claims.text: Adding tungsten to a high-entropy alloy induces nanoscale precipitate formation.
The resulting nanoscale precipitates enhance elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
The proposed intervention is the addition of 1–2 at.% tungsten during alloy manufacturing.
The hypothesized operating range is approximately 650–750°C under mechanical loading and creep conditions.
Tungsten addition promotes nucleation of finely dispersed precipitates.
The precipitates may be Laves-phase particles.
The tungsten-induced precipitates remain stable at elevated temperature.
Finely dispersed precipitates obstruct dislocation motion.
Obstruction of dislocation motion increases elevated-temperature yield strength.
Obstruction of dislocation motion retards elevated-temperature creep.
The tungsten-modified alloy will have greater yield strength than the tungsten-free baseline in the 650–750°C range.
The tungsten-modified alloy will have a lower creep rate than the tungsten-free baseline in the 650–750°C range.
The elevated-temperature yield-strength improvement may exceed 20%.
The benefit is not necessarily expected at low temperatures or for properties unrelated to strength and creep resistance.
The magnitude of improvement and optimal tungsten concentration depend on the alloy system and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The >20% yield-strength improvement is presented as a tentative example and the exact magnitude is explicitly uncertain, but the falsification rule treats less than approximately 20% improvement as sufficient to falsify the hypothesis. This converts a provisional estimate into a hard threshold.
